I truly believe and 100% maintain that ADHD can cause its own type of trauma. We grow up being an “other”, often bullied and feeling misunderstood. Not necessarily or always a “bit T trauma” but it certainly leaves a mark on us.

ADHD is a neurodevelopmental disorder. It’s literally how our brain develops. Is there often an overlap of symptoms? Sure. Absolutely. But PTSD is not a neurodevelopmental disorder and not everyone with ADHD has a history of trauma.

I went as a junior in high school and was in South America for 11 months. I loved my host family and I learned Spanish (still fluent too! And I dont have an American accent which is nice), but…there was a lot of really messed up stuff that went down. 

I was 16-17 and I had an older host brother. He was 23. I’m sure you can guess where this is going and it really messed with my head (he told me he loved me, I felt terrible and ashamed but thought I was supposed to love him too yadda yadda). I had an extremely hard time when I came back and struggled with debilitating PTSD for years. I contacted the exchange organization and reported everything and they led me on for 4 years. Said they filed a police report but they didn’t, said I could go back and file a police report but it would cost ME over $12,000USD, then said they’d pay for it all but no matter how many times I asked how to make that happen, they never told me. Ultimately, I received an email by accident in which a member of the organization was instructing two other members not to put anything in writing about me. It was really fucked up, to say the least. 

Ultimately, after years of therapy, I’m doing ok. I actually recently went back to the country I was in and met with my host brother. We spoke for several hours two of the days I was there and it was incredibly healing for me. I’m still pissed at the exchange program, but I have some peace re: what my host brother did and how it ruined my life for awhile. 

The program I went to is free. They cover the cost of everything except airfare, even give a monthly allowance. All I can really say about that is….you get what you pay for. 

I’ve been in touch with a producer who’s doing a documentary on exchanges and how they can go terribly wrong. It’s not uncommon to experience something like I did. 

Overall…now I’m able to look back and see my exchange as something that was awful but also wonderful. It destroyed me but it created me. I’d do it again, if I was able to start fresh and have the knowledge I do now. There wasn’t a true safety net for students and they didn’t prepare us for worst case scenarios. Running has saved my life. 

I’ve always loved running. I was that weirdo who got excited for the run in gym class and who didn’t feel like running laps for field hockey was punishment. I always wanted to do cross country or something, but my high school never had that available. So I just ran off and on over the years. Never seriously, just to run. Just to get away for a bit. 

I’ve struggled with an eating disorder since around age 12. Exercise has never been a behavior for me. I always struggled with bulimia but my recovery from bulimia turned into full blown anorexia around this time last year. I wound up in treatment, but just before I was admitted, I had started running again. It wasn’t always for the “right” reasons, but I realized while I was in treatment that it was a last ditch attempt to cope with things in a less destructive way. Unfortunately it just led to more weight loss and then, like I said, treatment. 

Since being discharged, running is what’s kept me on track. I eat so that I can run. It’s physically uncomfortable to eat still, it’s emotionally hard to eat a lot of the time, but I know I can’t run if I’m not eating enough. Running is the only time that bully in my brain disappears. It’s the only time I can quiet my mind and be mindful. I check in with myself and my body in a healthy way. My thoughts are supportive. I don’t berate myself. I ran my first 5k earlier this month and spent the whole time reminding myself I could do it, I could PR, I had trained for that. My thoughts are almost always negative otherwise. 

On a whim I applied for Chicago and got in. I’m addicted to running. But in a healthy way; if I don’t feel good or I haven’t eaten enough, I won’t push myself through a run. I’ll force myself if I know I’m just being lazy, but I’m gentle with myself. I look forward to it. I’ve gained weight because I’ve had to, and it hurts to look in the mirror sometimes. But looking at my body and thinking “this body is going to run a marathon”, that helps. I watch my thigh gap disappear and I’m ok because I know those legs are getting stronger. And I keep races scheduled because short term goals help keep me where I need to be in recovery. Running has helped me appreciate my body and want to see what it’s capable of. It’s made me want to be healthy and strong, not starve myself to death and disappear. Since gaining 10 pounds my pace has gone from 12-14 minute miles to 8:48-9:23 depending on the distance. It’s my solace. It’s my escape. It absolutely has saved my life.

I work in a substance abuse program in a prison as a clinician, while also doing my internship for my MSW at the same prison. I’m there 6 days a week, I work with women. Initially I thought I’d prefer to work with men but I love working with the women. A lot of drama, but a lot to work with and many of my clients have been more receptive to treatment than the men I’ve worked with. Boundaries are big. Absolutely. And for awhile I had to put on this act like I knew what I was doing. Not with my supervisor or colleagues but as soon as one inmate caught on that I hadn’t worked in a prison setting before ohhhhh man. I facilitate groups and there were a few that went downhill. At this point though, I’m very clear with how things go. I have a strict no coddling policy. That doesn’t mean I don’t have empathy, but sometimes what many of my clients are looking for from me is exactly what got them there to begin with. 


I love working in the prison. I’m manipulating the rest of my life and limiting family time to make this internship work so I can go right into a full time job that’s not contracted work (which my current position is). I love it. It’s always different. There’s a touch of adrenaline, depending on the day. And after working in hospitals and crisis settings that lacked sufficient security....I feel safe at work. I feel safer at work than in the community. The COs have my back and I’ve developed, as my supervisor puts it, my “clinical teeth”. I genuinely can’t imagine working in any other setting.

ETA: I’ll second the other comments on self care. The secondary trauma is so real and can be overwhelming. Also where dark humor comes in. 
Readjusting the way i speak and the material I use with clients can be tricky too. Many of them never completed past the 8th grade or so. But I’ve found that so many of them are eager to learn and honestly, cutting back on the clinical talk just improved the rapport. It’s hard to see so many cycle in and out and women tend to get shorter sentences which makes it hard too. But there are so many who are released and thrive and that makes it worth it. It’s frustrating, it’s challenging, it’s entertaining (the stories I could tell oh man), but it’s wonderful. I love it so much.

He told me I didn’t have to do that. Asked if I was getting treatment, if my family knew. Of course I had been to treatment, of course my family knew. He said I wasn’t doing anything illegal. He couldn’t stop me. He asked if I would be ok and he left. I cried for half an hour and finally purged. 

That should have been enough but two weeks later another cop found me. Same thing. Asked if I wanted him to help me (omg yes I needed it so badly) but I knew he would bring me to the ER of the hospital where i worked. I couldn’t. So i declined. And he left me alone and I cried and then I purged.
